rules.quote: Read your text aloud. If you run out of breath or stumble over a sentence, it is probably too long or complex. You can check the readability of your text using the Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch– Kincaid Grade Level tools available in Microsoft Word.
rules.rule: Check that sentences are not too long or complex; readability can be checked with the Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level tools.

check.notes: Advice to authors; a readability score can be reported for information only. The guide sets no numeric threshold (the project sentence-length cap is a client setting, not FAOSTYLE). "Flesch– Kincaid" is split across lines 686-687 in the conversion.

rules.quote: Remember that the introduction, conclusion and summary may be the only sections that your audience reads in full. Take special care to ensure that these are well written and succinct.
rules.rule: Make sure the introduction, conclusion and summary are well written and succinct.

rules.rule: Use plain language and a clear style, avoiding ambiguity.

rules.quote: Opt for shorter, simpler words rather than long phrases, e.g. because instead of due to the fact that, or needs instead of has a requirement for.

check.notes: Only the two pairs printed in the guide (plus the plural verb form of the second). Other wordy phrases need the agent.

rules.quote: Beware of buzzwords (e.g. synergy, visioning), as these may quickly fade from usage.

rules.quote: Avoid jargon, colloquialisms or slang; where necessary, explain the meaning.

rules.quote: Avoid unnecessary and vague adverbs and intensifiers (e.g. hopefully, really, very).
rules.rule: Avoid unnecessary or vague adverbs and intensifiers such as hopefully, really and very.

check.notes: Flags every occurrence of the three printed examples; "very" is frequent and often acceptable, so the editor decides whether it is unnecessary.

rules.rule: Prefer the active voice to the passive voice.

rules.quote: Avoid double negatives: It is common to ... is better than It is not uncommon to ....

check.notes: Heuristic list of not + negative-prefix adjective; the guide prints only "not uncommon". Other double negatives (e.g. not without) need the agent.

rules.quote: Use terminology accurately and consistently.

rules.quote: Editors of multi-author books should ensure that chapters by different authors employ the same terms for the same concepts.

rules.quote: Replace imprecise verbs (e.g. do, make, get, enhance) with more precise alternatives (e.g. perform, create, obtain, improve).

rules.rule: When describing quantities, avoid a few, some, many, enough, several and a number of.

rules.quote: Quotation marks should be used only for direct quotes and scare quotes (expressions that are colloquial, ironic or purposely use non-standard language).
rules.rule: Use quotation marks only for direct quotes and scare quotes.

check.notes: Typical misuse: quotation marks for emphasis, titles or terms being defined.

rules.quote: Scare quotes should be used rarely.
rules.rule: Use scare quotes rarely.

rules.quote: Always use double quotation marks (“) rather than single quotation marks (‘) unless there is a quote within a quote, e.g. Baresi (1998, p. 72) reports that “farmers complain about ‘unofficial’ agents.”
rules.rule: Use double quotation marks; single quotation marks only for a quote within a quote.

check.notes: Matches from the start of the paragraph to a curly single-quoted span that is not inside a double-quoted span (the match span is wide; report the ‘...’ part). Straight single quotes are not checked because they cannot be told from apostrophes. A double-quoted passage that continues over a paragraph break defeats the nesting check.

correct: Baresi (1998, p. 72) reports that “farmers complain about ‘unofficial’ agents.”

rules.quote: When a quotation is approximately three lines or longer, indent the quotation and do not use quotation marks.
rules.rule: Set quotations of about three lines or more as indented block quotes without quotation marks.

check.notes: About three lines is approximated as 250 characters (roughly 40 words). Indentation itself is only visible in the DOCX.

rules.quote: Semicolons are used to separate independent clauses that have different subjects and are not connected by a conjunction.
rules.rule: Use a semicolon between independent clauses with different subjects not joined by a conjunction.

rules.quote: A semicolon is followed by an initial lower case letter.
rules.rule: Start the word after a semicolon in lower case.

check.notes: Only flags common sentence-starting words, so proper nouns after a semicolon are not flagged. Citation strings such as "(FAO, 2019; The World Bank, 2020)" are excluded by the year look-ahead.

rules.quote: In long sentences comprising a series of complex clauses, at least one of which contains a comma, semicolons may replace commas
rules.rule: In a long series of complex clauses, at least one containing a comma, semicolons may replace commas.

correct: The meeting covered IT, human resources and capacity building; reviewed the minutes of the previous meeting and proposed amendments to the agenda; and explored concerns raised by the participants in relation to the new information-sharing platform and software upgrades.

rules.quote: The slash / should generally be avoided in running text.
rules.rule: Avoid slashes in running text, except for the accepted uses (yes/no, 2008/09, mg/kg).

check.notes: Flags word/word with words of three or more letters (so most unit ratios such as mg/kg, t/ha are skipped). URLs and paths are excluded by the look-arounds, and FAO photo credits (© FAO/Name, section 12.1) are skipped. and/or (PUN-5_12-003) and he/she (WRT-3_3_2-004) have their own entries.

exceptions.quote: to designate mutually exclusive alternatives such as yes/no or pass/fail, particularly in tables or forms;
exceptions.note: Mutually exclusive alternatives.

exceptions.quote: to denote periods such as academic or fiscal years, e.g. the 2008/09 financial year or the Australian summer of 2009/10; and
exceptions.note: Academic/fiscal periods.

exceptions.quote: to indicate per between units of measurement and values, e.g. 12 mg/kg.
exceptions.note: "per" between units.

rules.quote: When used, there should be no space before or after the slash.
rules.rule: No space before or after a slash.

rules.quote: Try to rephrase any sentences that have been written with and/or, as it may cause confusion and difficulty in translation.
rules.rule: Rephrase sentences containing and/or.

rules.quote: Leave only one space after the full stop between sentences.
rules.rule: Use one space after a full stop between sentences.

rules.quote: Use a non-breaking space between numbers and units;
rules.rule: Use a non-breaking space between a number and its unit.

check.notes: Matches an ordinary space (U+0020); a non-breaking space (U+00A0 or U+202F) passes. The conversion of the guide shows ordinary spaces in its own examples (e.g. "Figure 1", "12 kg"), presumably because the non-breaking spaces were lost, so those examples are not used as tests. Run on the DOCX text, not on markdown that may have normalized spaces. Compound modifiers take a hyphen instead (PUN-5_8-009, "a 15-kg bag").

rules.quote: for figure, table and box numbers (e.g. Figure 1);
rules.rule: Use a non-breaking space in figure, table and box numbers (Figure 1).

rules.quote: after e.g. and i.e.;
rules.rule: Use a non-breaking space after e.g. and i.e.

rules.quote: and in other similar cases.
rules.rule: Use non-breaking spaces in other similar cases where a break would separate linked items.

check.notes: "Similar cases" is not defined; candidates are currency codes and amounts (USD 2), p./pp. and page numbers, No. and number.
